stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Renata Villacorta's 2011 novel The Fourth Morning. Ines, a linguist, is recording Aldo, one of the last fluent speakers of a mountain dialect.

For three mornings Ines had arrived with her printed lists (every pronoun, every tense, every way to say carry), and for three mornings Aldo had answered each prompt with a story about his brother or a stubborn mule. She had begun marking those minutes in her notebook as lost. On the fourth morning, however, transcribing the tale of the mule, she found in it four tenses her lists had never thought to ask for. After that she left the lists in her bag and simply asked him what happened next.
choices: To portray a speaker's reluctance to answer a researcher's questions until he comes to trust her
To show a researcher giving up her scholarly aims so that she can simply enjoy a speaker's stories
To depict a researcher realizing that what she had written off as a distraction was serving her purpose
To suggest that a researcher's printed lists were flawed because they misrepresented a dialect's grammar
explanation: The setup line puts the focus on Ines. Across the excerpt she treats Aldo's stories as wasted time (she marks those minutes "as lost"). Then, after "however," she finds in one story four tenses her lists never asked about, and she switches to asking for more stories. So the excerpt shows her coming to see that the supposed distraction was actually giving her the data she came for. Choice C names the right person and the right change.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ines to Aldo and added a motive the text never gives. Aldo answers every prompt, just with stories, and the excerpt never mentions trust. This is the subtype's main trap: it uses the right characters but makes the wrong person the subject.

B.why: You saw that Ines changes her approach, which is the key insight, but you misread why. She puts the lists away because the stories gave her four tenses her lists missed. The change serves her research goals. It doesn't abandon them.

D.why: The text says the lists never thought to ask for certain tenses, so they were incomplete. It never says they contained errors or misrepresented the grammar. On top of that, the excerpt is about Ines's realization, not about judging her materials.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Teodor Lisk's 2016 poem "Annealing." The speaker addresses a young apprentice in a glassworks.

You flinch when the oven door shuts on your bowl,
as if the waiting were a verdict. It is not.
Glass that is hurried from fire into air
keeps the fire inside it as strain,
and one day breaks for no reason anyone can see.
So we cool it by hours, a degree at a time,
and what comes out looks no different—
only able, now, to be dropped and stay whole.
You are being cooled the same way. Let it take its time.
choices: To warn an apprentice that rushing her work will cause the glass she makes to crack and break
To explain the technical process by which glassmakers relieve the internal strain in their glass
To describe the speaker's lasting regret over the work she ruined when she was an apprentice
To reassure an apprentice that a period of waiting she dreads is what will make her resilient
explanation: The poem is addressed to the apprentice, so focus on what it says to her. She "flinch[es]" at the waiting, and the speaker answers right away: "It is not" a verdict. The description of slow cooling leads to the last line, "You are being cooled the same way," which turns the glass into a picture of her own slow training. Just as slow cooling makes the bowl able to "stay whole," the waiting she fears is making her stronger. The tone is comforting, which matches Choice D.

A.why: You noticed that hurried glass breaks, which is the key detail, but you finished the thought in the wrong tone. The apprentice isn't rushing anything. She is anxious about waiting, and the speaker calms her down ("It is not") instead of warning her. Turning an encouraging poem into a warning is this subtype's tone trap.

B.why: You described what most of the lines are about instead of what the poem does. The annealing process is there to set up the comparison in the last line about the apprentice. Someone who skipped that line could have written this choice, and that is a sign it misses the purpose.

C.why: The poem never mentions the speaker's own past failures or regrets. This choice invents a backstory and also moves the focus away from the apprentice the poem is speaking to.
